criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: LLC citizenship alleged via member citizenship, not state of formation
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint explicitly addresses LLC citizenship in paragraph 5, stating: 'For purposes of diversity jurisdiction, a limited liability company is a citizen of every state of which each of its members is a citizen.' It then identifies the members (Marcus J. Harwell and Elena Rosario-Vega), alleges their domicile/citizenship in Texas, and concludes Westlake is a citizen of Texas only. The complaint does not rely on state of formation (Delaware) for citizenship purposes. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Complaint cites or reflects Carden v. Arkoma LLC citizenship rule
criteria_results.reasoning: The filing issues memo (Section 2.1) explicitly addresses the LLC citizenship rule, explaining that the intake memo incorrectly applied the corporate citizenship test (state of organization + principal place of business) to Westlake LLC, and that in the Fifth Circuit an LLC's citizenship is determined by the citizenship of each of its members traced through every layer, citing Harvey v. Grey Wolf Drilling Co., 542 F.3d 1077, 1080 (5th Cir. 2008). The complaint itself also reflects this awareness by leaving bracketed placeholders requiring confirmation of each member's domicile and noting that 'a limited liability company is a citizen of every state of which each of its members is a citizen.' While Carden v. Arkoma is not cited by name, the rule it established is clearly articulated and applied. The criterion states the rule can be shown by 'expressly explaining the LLC-member citizenship rule,' which both documents do.

criteria_results.title: Diversity jurisdiction: Graydon citizenship properly alleged
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 6 of the complaint explicitly states: 'Defendant Graydon Strategic Advisors Inc. is a New York corporation with its principal place of business at 450 Park Avenue, 22nd Floor, New York, New York 10022. Graydon is a citizen of New York.' This correctly alleges both the state of incorporation (New York) and the principal place of business (New York), satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Diversity jurisdiction: Amount in controversy exceeds $75,000
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 9 of the complaint explicitly states: 'The amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs; the milestone payments alone that Westlake seeks to recover total $750,000.' The complaint also details damages including $750,000 in milestone payments, up to $5,000,000 in lost management fees, lost carried interest, approximately $1,200,000 in consequential costs, $750,000 in disgorgement, forfeiture of at least $280,000 in retainers, and exemplary damages — collectively far exceeding $75,000. The criterion requires the complaint to allege the amount exceeds $75,000 and reference a comparable figure to ~$14,730,000. While the complaint does not aggregate all damages into a single '$14,730,000' figure, it clearly alleges amounts well in excess of $75,000 and the threshold is explicitly addressed. The criterion states PASS if the complaint alleges the amount exceeds $75,000 and references total estimated damages of approximately $14,730,000 'or a comparable figure that clearly exceeds the threshold.' The complaint's itemized damages clearly exceed $75,000 and the jurisdictional allegation is present.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Forum selection clause cited for venue and personal jurisdiction
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint explicitly cites PAA Section 12.2 in both the personal jurisdiction section (paragraphs 10-12) and the venue section (paragraph 13). Paragraph 10 quotes Section 12.2 as Graydon's irrevocable submission to 'the exclusive jurisdiction' of 'the state or federal courts located in Dallas County, Texas.' Paragraph 13 states venue is proper 'by agreement under PAA Section 12.2, in which Graydon waived any objection to venue in Dallas County, including on grounds of forum non conveniens.' The forum selection clause is thus referenced for both personal jurisdiction and venue.

criteria_results.title: Venue: Northern District of Texas alleged under 28 U.S.C. § 1391
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 13 of the complaint explicitly alleges venue under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2), stating that 'a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claims occurred in Dallas County, Texas,' and also references the contractual forum-selection clause in PAA Section 12.2. The complaint is filed in the Northern District of Texas, Dallas Division, as shown in the caption. Both bases for venue are properly alleged.

criteria_results.title: Personal jurisdiction: Minimum contacts alleged in addition to forum selection clause
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 10 of the complaint explicitly alleges personal jurisdiction over Graydon on two independent bases: (1) the forum-selection clause in PAA Section 12.2, under which Graydon irrevocably submitted to the exclusive jurisdiction of Dallas County courts; and (2) minimum contacts with Texas, specifically that Graydon contracted with a Dallas-based principal, sent personnel to Dallas for meetings on multiple occasions, delivered monthly activity reports and milestone certifications to Westlake in Dallas, and accepted approximately $3,130,000 in payments from Westlake's Dallas accounts. Paragraph 11 similarly alleges specific jurisdiction over Trevor Graydon based on his directing fraudulent communications into Texas and his close relationship to the PAA's forum-selection clause. Both bases are clearly pleaded, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Fiduciary duty claim grounded in PAA Section 8.1 express acknowledgment
criteria_results.reasoning: Count II (Breach of Fiduciary Duty) explicitly references PAA Section 8.1 in paragraph 57, stating that 'Graydon owed Westlake fiduciary duties both because Graydon expressly acknowledged that it acted in a fiduciary capacity (PAA § 8.1)' and the factual allegations in paragraph 24 quote Section 8.1 at length, including the duties of loyalty, candor, and good faith, the duty to act solely in Westlake's best interests, and the duty to make full disclosure of conflicts. The fiduciary duty count clearly references the express contractual acknowledgment in PAA Section 8.1.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Fiduciary duty claim also alleges common law agency-based fiduciary relationship
criteria_results.reasoning: Count II (paragraphs 56-59) explicitly pleads both bases for fiduciary duty: (1) the contractual acknowledgment in PAA § 8.1, and (2) the common law agency relationship. Paragraph 57 states: 'Graydon owed Westlake fiduciary duties both because Graydon expressly acknowledged that it acted in a fiduciary capacity (PAA § 8.1) and because, as Westlake's agent for the solicitation of Capital Commitments (PAA § 13.7), Graydon owed Westlake the formal fiduciary duties that the common law imposes on an agent toward its principal, including duties of loyalty, candor, full disclosure, and to refrain from self-dealing and from competing with the principal.' This clearly pleads an independent common law agency-based fiduciary relationship in addition to the contractual basis.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Complaint addresses Graydon Capital Solutions as related entity
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint names Graydon Capital Solutions LLC as a defendant (paragraph 8), alleges it is an Affiliate of Graydon Strategic Advisors under the PAA (paragraph 29), alleges it acted through Graydon's personnel and infrastructure with no separate existence (paragraph 28), and asserts in Count III that GCS knowingly participated in Graydon's breach of fiduciary duty as a joint tortfeasor (paragraphs 60-63). The complaint also alleges GCS is under common control with Graydon and wholly owned by Graydon's principal (paragraph 29), and that it acted as an instrumentality/agent of Graydon and Trevor Graydon. This directly addresses the separate-entity defense raised in Graydon's response letter by providing multiple legal theories connecting GCS's conduct to the other defendants.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Issues memo flags separate-entity defense and recommends strategy
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 4.2 of the memo explicitly addresses Graydon Capital Solutions LLC and discusses the separate-entity/jurisdiction risk. It notes that 'GCS signed nothing with Westlake' and discusses jurisdictional theories including alter ego. Section 10 also addresses the '"Separate entity" / § 7.4 does not reach affiliates' defense. The memo discusses alter ego as a veil-piercing theory, agency attribution through Trevor Graydon, and the 'closely related' non-signatory doctrine. It explicitly states the complaint 'deliberately does not plead alter ego as a stand-alone theory' but notes it can be added after discovery, and explains why veil piercing may not be needed given the contract's affiliate language and direct tort theories. The separate-entity defense is clearly identified as a litigation risk with recommended strategies to overcome it.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Fraud claim states who, what, when, where, how per Rule 9(b)
criteria_results.reasoning: The fraud count (Count IV) and the supporting factual allegations satisfy Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirements. WHO: Paragraphs 37, 65-66 identify Nathaniel Pruitt as the preparer and Trevor Graydon as the approver/signer of each certification and report, and note Trevor Graydon's personal participation. WHAT: Paragraphs 38-41 and 65 specify the exact false statements — the May 8, 2023 certification claimed $50.5M when actual commitments were $35M (with GPPERS inflated to $8M based on a single introductory call); the September 9, 2023 certification claimed $101.5M when actual commitments were $35M; the March 8, 2024 certification claimed $152M when actual commitments were $87.5M; plus the specific false statements about Harborview postponing review, GPPERS pending board approval, and no conflicts requiring disclosure. WHEN: Specific dates are given — May 8, 2023; September 9, 2023; January 9, 2024; March 8, 2024. WHERE/HOW: Paragraph 37 states each report was delivered from Graydon in New York to Westlake in Dallas; paragraph 44 notes Westlake relied on them. The complaint meets all four Rule 9(b) elements with the required specificity.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Fraud count references Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b) heightened standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint does not explicitly cite Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b) anywhere in the document. However, the fraud count (Count IV) is structured with considerable particularity: it identifies specific speakers (Pruitt and Trevor Graydon), specific false statements, specific dates (May 8, 2023; September 9, 2023; January 9, 2024; March 8, 2024), specific dollar amounts, and the mechanism of the fraud. The allegations in paragraphs 38-41 provide the 'who, what, when, where, and how' framework that Rule 9(b) requires. The criterion states PASS if the complaint 'explicitly acknowledges or structures the fraud claim to satisfy Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b)'s heightened pleading requirement, either by citing Rule 9(b) or by clearly organizing the allegations to meet the who, what, when, where, and how framework.' The complaint does not cite Rule 9(b) by name, but it does clearly organize the fraud allegations with the requisite particularity — specific dates, specific statements, specific actors, specific amounts, and specific reliance. The criterion allows passing based on structure alone without explicit citation. The fraud allegations are organized with sufficient particularity to satisfy the 9(b) framework, even without an explicit reference to the rule itself.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Economic loss rule addressed in issues memo
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8 of the memo explicitly addresses the economic-loss rule as a potential defense Graydon will raise, noting that 'Graydon will argue that misstatements made during performance are only contract breaches.' It then discusses the exceptions: (a) independent statements of fact made to obtain money, (b) independent fiduciary duty as an agent existing regardless of contract (citing Chapman Custom Homes), and (c) claims against Trevor Graydon and GCS not arising from any contract with them. It also cites Formosa Plastics Corp. USA v. Presidio Eng'rs & Contractors, Inc., 960 S.W.2d 41, 47 (Tex. 1998), directly addressing the fraudulent inducement exception. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Fraud claim framed to survive economic loss rule
criteria_results.reasoning: Count IV (paragraphs 64-69) explicitly addresses the economic loss rule. Paragraph 69 states: 'Because Defendants' fraud is independent of Graydon's contractual promises and arose from its fiduciary relationship with Westlake, and because Westlake seeks recovery of benefits fraudulently obtained, Westlake's fraud claim is not barred by the economic loss rule.' The fraud claim is framed as arising from the fiduciary relationship (an independent duty), not merely from contractual representations. The complaint also pleads fraud by nondisclosure based on the fiduciary/agency relationship (paragraph 67), which under Texas law creates an independent duty to disclose separate from contract. These framings — fraud independent of contract and fraud arising from fiduciary duty — are recognized Texas exceptions to the economic loss rule. The claim is not pled purely as breach of contractual representations.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Unjust enrichment pled as alternative claim
criteria_results.reasoning: Count V (Unjust Enrichment and Money Had and Received) expressly pleads the unjust enrichment claim against Graydon in the alternative: 'In the alternative, and only to the extent the Court determines that any Milestone Payment or other compensation paid to Graydon falls outside the PAA or that the PAA is unenforceable in any relevant respect, Graydon has been unjustly enriched...' This language acknowledges the express-contract limitation under Texas law and confines the unjust enrichment claim against Graydon to circumstances where the PAA does not govern or is unenforceable. The primary unjust enrichment claim against GCS and Trevor Graydon (non-parties to the PAA) is appropriately pled as a standalone claim since no express contract between them and Westlake covers the subject matter. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Unjust enrichment targets Graydon Capital Solutions' Ridgecrest fees
criteria_results.reasoning: Count V (Unjust Enrichment and Money Had and Received) specifically targets GCS and Trevor Graydon for the Ridgecrest introduction fees. Paragraph 71 states that GCS and Trevor Graydon are not parties to the PAA and that they obtained fees from Ridgecrest by fraud and through participation in Graydon's breach of fiduciary duty. Paragraph 73 requests disgorgement of these amounts and imposition of a constructive trust over the Ridgecrest introduction fees. The $750,000 figure (1.5% × $50M) is referenced in paragraph 36 and paragraph 49, and the prayer for relief paragraph (d) specifically requests disgorgement of 'all introduction fees and other benefits obtained by GCS and Trevor Graydon from Ridgecrest on account of Fund III Investors, presently estimated at $750,000.' The unjust enrichment claim is clearly directed at the Ridgecrest fees falling outside the PAA, not merely at payments made under the PAA.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Discovery rule alleged for fraud statute of limitations
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 78 explicitly invokes the discovery rule, alleges that injuries were 'inherently undiscoverable,' and states that 'accrual of all claims was deferred until at least April 17, 2024, when Westlake first learned facts suggesting Graydon's involvement with Ridgecrest.' Paragraph 45 describes the April 17, 2024 Chicago conference conversation between Rosario-Vega and the Northshore CIO as the moment of discovery. Paragraph 46 confirms that before that date Westlake had no knowledge of the Ridgecrest Agreement. The complaint thus satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: All claims within applicable statutes of limitations
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8 of the memo explicitly addresses statutes of limitations. It correctly states that breach of contract, fraud, and breach of fiduciary duty each carry a four-year limitations period under Texas law (citing Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §§ 16.004(a)(4)-(5), 16.051). It also notes that unjust enrichment carries a two-year period. The memo confirms that the earliest act (May 15, 2023) is still within two years of an August 2024 filing, so nothing is time-barred. It also pleads the discovery rule and fraudulent concealment with April 17, 2024 as the discovery date. The criterion requires analysis confirming all claims are timely, and the memo does this thoroughly.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Issues memo flags speculative damages risk for carried interest
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo does flag the carried interest claim as problematic in Section 6 (Damages table) and Section 3 (errors table). It notes the math is wrong ($50M × 1.185^7 ≈ $164.1M, not $170.3M), that the model applies carry to a net IRR which is circular, and that the '$7.5M conservative' figure has no stated method. It recommends retaining a testifying damages expert and pleads no dollar figure for carry. However, the criterion specifically requires the memo to identify the speculative nature tied to projected fund performance from historical Fund I and Fund II returns (average 18.5% net IRR), and to note the risk of a Daubert challenge or motion to dismiss, and to recommend grounding the claim in expert methodology and/or historical performance data. The memo does recommend retaining a damages expert, which partially addresses the 'expert methodology' recommendation. But it does not mention Daubert challenges or motions to dismiss related to the carried interest claim, and does not specifically identify the speculative nature as stemming from projected fund performance based on historical Fund I/II returns. The memo focuses on arithmetic errors and methodological circularity rather than the broader speculative/Daubert risk. The criterion requires flagging the speculative nature due to projected performance from historical returns AND noting Daubert/MTD risk. The memo falls short on these specific points.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Complaint includes non-speculative damages theories
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint includes all four concrete damages categories: (a) $750,000 in milestone payments (paragraphs 48(a), prayer (b)); (b) lost management fees of up to $5,000,000 on $50M diverted commitments at 2.0% over five years (paragraph 48(c)); (c) retainer disgorgement of not less than $280,000 for 8 months (paragraphs 48(b), prayer (c)); and (d) $1,200,000 in consequential costs (paragraph 48(e)). The milestone disgorgement and lost management fee figures both appear explicitly. The complaint does not rely solely on carried interest.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Trevor Graydon named as individual defendant
criteria_results.reasoning: Trevor Graydon is explicitly named as an individual defendant in the caption, parties section (paragraph 7), and throughout the complaint. He is named in Count III (knowing participation in breach of fiduciary duty), Count IV (fraud), Count V (unjust enrichment), and Count VI (injunction). The complaint details his personal participation including signing the Ridgecrest Agreement as sole manager of GCS, personally approving false reports, personally promoting Cascadia Fund IV to GPPERS and Northshore, and executing the PAA on Graydon's behalf.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Personal liability theory articulated for Trevor Graydon
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint articulates multiple theories for Trevor Graydon's individual liability. In paragraph 66, it explicitly states the participation theory: 'A corporate agent is personally liable for fraudulent or tortious acts that he commits or in which he knowingly participates, even when acting on the corporation's behalf.' The complaint also alleges he personally signed and approved false certifications and reports, personally promoted Cascadia Fund IV to Fund III prospects, personally executed the Ridgecrest Agreement as sole manager of GCS, and personally directed the diversion scheme. Count III (knowing participation in breach of fiduciary duty) and Count IV (fraud) are both asserted against Trevor Graydon individually with specific factual allegations supporting personal liability. The complaint clearly articulates the participation/personal participation theory for individual officer liability.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Non-solicitation 12-month tail provision alleged
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint explicitly references PAA Section 7.4's non-solicitation clause in paragraph 23, stating 'During the Term and for twelve months thereafter (the "Restricted Period")' and that 'Because the Term expired on July 18, 2024, the Restricted Period runs through July 18, 2025.' Count VI (paragraphs 74-76) further alleges ongoing violation of Section 7.4 as a basis for injunctive relief, noting the Ridgecrest Agreement remains in effect through July 31, 2025, giving Defendants a continuing incentive to divert remaining Fund III prospects. The prayer for relief also requests an injunction through July 18, 2025 with possible extension. All required elements are present.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Complaint requests injunctive relief
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint includes Count VI titled 'PERMANENT INJUNCTION TO ENFORCE PAA SECTION 7.4' (paragraphs 74-76) which explicitly requests injunctive relief to enforce the non-solicitation provision and prevent Defendants from diverting Fund III investors to competing funds. The prayer for relief at paragraph (g) also requests 'A permanent injunction as described in Count VI.' Count VI also reserves the right to move for preliminary relief. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Irreparable harm alleged to support injunctive relief
criteria_results.reasoning: Count VI (paragraphs 75-76) explicitly alleges irreparable harm beyond monetary damages. Paragraph 76 states that 'the loss of institutional investor relationships and fundraising momentum is irreparable and not readily compensable in damages, as Graydon agreed in PAA Section 12.4.' This goes beyond mere monetary damages by pointing to the unique, non-fungible nature of institutional investor relationships and fundraising momentum. The complaint also references the contractual acknowledgment of irreparable harm in PAA Section 12.4, and paragraph 25 notes the PAA provides that breach 'would cause irreparable harm' entitling Westlake to injunctive relief without bond. These allegations satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: DISTRACTOR_001: Texas governing law treated as straightforward
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint simply states that Texas law governs per PAA Section 12.1 without raising any conflict-of-laws concerns. The filing-issues memo does not flag the Texas choice-of-law provision as a significant risk or vulnerability requiring analysis. The memo discusses many issues (jurisdiction, damages, economic-loss rule, etc.) but treats the Texas governing law clause as settled and unproblematic. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: DISTRACTOR_002: FINRA registration not treated as jurisdictional obstacle
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint includes Graydon's FINRA registration (CRD No. 298714) as a factual detail in paragraph 6 without treating it as a jurisdictional bar or mandatory arbitration obligation. The filing issues memo (Section 10) explicitly addresses FINRA arbitration and correctly states that 'FINRA arbitration is available at a customer's election, and Westlake has chosen court under § 12.2. Graydon cannot compel arbitration on that basis. Low risk.' Neither document incorrectly treats FINRA registration as requiring mandatory arbitration or as a barrier to federal court jurisdiction.

criteria_results.title: DISTRACTOR_003: Retainer payment calculation is clean
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint treats the retainer payments straightforwardly. It states the Monthly Retainer was $35,000 (PAA § 4.3) and calculates the disgorgement claim as 'Monthly Retainers of not less than $280,000 paid from November 2023 through June 2024' (8 months × $35,000 = $280,000). There is no fabricated dispute about payment timing, no challenge to the retainer amounts owed, and no artificial issue created around retainer payments. The calculation is clean and consistent with the criterion.

criteria_results.title: DISTRACTOR_004: Fund III hard cap not treated as material issue
criteria_results.reasoning: The $225M hard cap is mentioned only once in the complaint (paragraph 15) as background context describing Fund III's terms: 'Fund III is a Delaware limited partnership formed on November 15, 2022, with a target of $200 million in capital commitments and a hard cap of $225 million.' It is not treated as a legal issue, defense, or complication for any claim or damages calculation. The filing issues memo does not mention the hard cap at all. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Breach of contract count: All material breaches alleged
criteria_results.reasoning: Count I (Breach of Contract against Graydon) at paragraph 53 explicitly alleges breaches of: (a) Section 7.2 — failure to disclose the Ridgecrest Agreement and the conflict of interest; (b) Section 7.3 — undisclosed referral arrangement; (c) Section 7.4 — soliciting, diverting, redirecting, and encouraging GPPERS, Harborview, and Northshore to invest in a Competing Fund; (d) Sections 4.2 and 5.3 — delivering materially false Milestone Certifications; and (e) Section 5.2 — delivering monthly activity reports that misstated investor status and omitted material developments. The exclusivity breach is addressed through the allegation that Graydon violated its role as 'sole and exclusive placement agent' by secretly working for a competing fund (PAA §§ 2.1-2.2 referenced in paragraph 16, and the conduct described throughout). All four required breach theories are present: (1) exclusivity/sole and exclusive placement agent role violated by secret competing arrangement, (2) non-solicitation (Section 7.4) explicitly alleged, (3) conflicts provision (Section 7.2) explicitly alleged, and (4) reporting obligation (false activity reports, Section 5.2) explicitly alleged. The criterion requires that no two or more of the four theories be omitted; here all four are present.

criteria_results.title: All three diverted investors identified with specifics
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint identifies all three diverted investors with the correct names and commitment amounts: (1) Great Plains Public Employees' Retirement System (GPPERS) — $25 million committed to Cascadia Fund IV in January 2024 (paragraphs 31-32); (2) Harborview Endowment Fund — $15 million committed in December 2023 (paragraphs 33); (3) Northshore Family Office LLC — $10 million committed in February 2024 (paragraph 34). The total of $50 million is also explicitly stated in paragraphs 2 and 36. All three investors are named, all commitment amounts are correct, and all timing details match the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Graydon-Ridgecrest Capital Introduction Agreement alleged with date
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 26 explicitly states: 'On August 1, 2023 --- six and a half months into the exclusive engagement --- Trevor Graydon executed, as "Sole Manager," a Capital Introduction Agreement between GCS and Ridgecrest (the "Ridgecrest Agreement").' Paragraph 30 states that neither Graydon nor Trevor Graydon ever disclosed the Ridgecrest Agreement to Westlake. The PAA exclusivity period ran from January 18, 2023 through July 18, 2024, and August 1, 2023 falls within that period (described as 'six and a half months into the exclusive engagement'). All three required elements are present: the agreement between GCS and Ridgecrest, the August 1, 2023 date, execution during the exclusivity period, and non-disclosure to Westlake.

criteria_results.title: Discovery narrative: April 2024 Chicago conference alleged
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 45 of the complaint explicitly alleges that on the evening of April 17, 2024, Ms. Rosario-Vega attended a networking reception at an institutional investor conference in Chicago, Illinois, where she spoke with Northshore's Chief Investment Officer, who stated that Northshore had committed $10 million to Cascadia Fund IV and that 'We went through Trevor's group --- his team at Graydon set up all the meetings with Ridgecrest.' All required elements are present: April 2024 date, Chicago conference, and the Northshore CIO's statement about committing to Cascadia Fund IV through Graydon's team.

criteria_results.title: Complaint includes four separate counts
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint contains six counts, not four. The four required counts are present: Count I (Breach of Contract), Count II (Breach of Fiduciary Duty), Count IV (Common-Law Fraud and Fraud by Nondisclosure), and Count V (Unjust Enrichment and Money Had and Received). However, the criterion requires exactly four separately numbered/titled counts matching those specific categories. The complaint has six counts total (adding Count III for Knowing Participation in Breach of Fiduciary Duty and Count VI for Permanent Injunction). The criterion states FAIL if any of the four required counts is missing — all four required counts ARE present. The criterion does not say the complaint must have ONLY four counts, just that it must contain those four. All four required counts exist as separately numbered and titled counts.

criteria_results.title: Complaint includes proper caption for Northern District of Texas
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint caption clearly identifies the court as 'IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE NORTHERN DISTRICT OF TEXAS DALLAS DIVISION,' names Westlake Capital Partners LLC as Plaintiff, and names Graydon Strategic Advisors Inc. as the first-listed Defendant. All required elements are present and correct.

criteria_results.title: Complaint includes jury demand
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint includes a jury demand in multiple places: the caption states 'JURY TRIAL DEMANDED', Section VIII is titled 'JURY DEMAND' and paragraph 79 states 'Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 38, Westlake demands a trial by jury on all issues so triable.'

criteria_results.title: Complaint includes attorney signature block
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint includes a signature block identifying Kendrick, Lyle & Strauss LLP with attorneys Catherine M. Aldridge and Jordan T. Nakamura at 1700 Pacific Avenue, Suite 3200, Dallas, Texas 75201. Both named attorneys are present and the firm address matches the required criterion.

criteria_results.title: Prayer for relief includes compensatory damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section IX includes item (a): 'Actual damages, including direct and consequential damages, in an amount to be proven at trial' and item (b): 'Recovery of the $750,000 in Milestone Payments.' The complaint also lists component damages categories in paragraph 48: (a) $750,000 in Milestone Payments, (b) Monthly Retainers of not less than $280,000, (c) lost management fees up to $5,000,000, (d) lost carried interest, and (e) consequential costs of approximately $1,200,000. The criterion requires either a total figure of approximately $14,730,000 or listing the component damages categories. The complaint lists the component categories in paragraph 48 and requests compensatory/actual damages in the prayer. However, the prayer itself does not reference a total figure of ~$14,730,000, nor does it explicitly list all the component categories (it just says 'actual damages...in an amount to be proven at trial'). The criterion says PASS if the prayer 'references a total damages figure of approximately $14,730,000 OR listing the component damages categories.' The component categories are listed in paragraph 48 (incorporated by reference into the counts), and the prayer requests actual damages. The prayer does reference the $750,000 milestone payments separately. The component categories are detailed in the factual allegations section (para 48) which is incorporated into each count. The prayer itself requests 'actual damages, including direct and consequential damages' plus separately the $750,000 milestone payments, forfeiture of $280,000+, disgorgement of $750,000, etc. The criterion is whether the prayer includes compensatory damages referencing the total figure or listing component categories. The prayer does list several component items (items a-e cover different damage types) and requests compensatory damages. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Prayer for relief includes disgorgement
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief explicitly requests disgorgement in multiple places: item (b) requests recovery of the $750,000 in Milestone Payments, item (d) requests 'Disgorgement of all introduction fees and other benefits obtained by GCS and Trevor Graydon from Ridgecrest on account of Fund III Investors, presently estimated at $750,000, and imposition of a constructive trust over such fees and their proceeds,' and item (c) requests forfeiture of compensation paid during the period of disloyalty. The complaint clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Prayer for relief includes punitive damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in Section IX explicitly includes '(f) Exemplary damages;' as one of the requested remedies. Additionally, Section VI is entirely dedicated to 'EXEMPLARY DAMAGES,' requesting exemplary damages against each Defendant under Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 41.003(a). Exemplary damages are the Texas statutory equivalent of punitive damages.

criteria_results.title: Prayer for relief includes attorneys' fees and costs
criteria_results.reasoning: The prayer for relief in section IX explicitly requests '(h) Reasonable attorneys' fees, expert fees, and costs under PAA Sections 10.1 and 12.3, Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code § 38.001, and other applicable law.' This clearly satisfies the criterion of requesting attorneys' fees and costs.

criteria_results.title: Factual allegations organized chronologically
criteria_results.reasoning: The factual allegations in Section IV are organized into clearly labeled subsections that follow a chronological progression: (A) Westlake and Fund III background, (B) the PAA executed January 18, 2023, (C) Trevor Graydon's secret alignment with Ridgecrest beginning August 1, 2023, (D) the diversion of investors through late 2023 and early 2024, (E) the false reports and milestone certifications from May 2023 through March 2024 presented in date order, (F) discovery of the scheme on April 17, 2024, and (G) damages. The narrative moves from fund formation and contract execution, through the fundraising period and the secret competing arrangement, through the specific false certifications in chronological order (May 2023, September 2023, January 2024, March 2024), to discovery and the demand letter in June 2024. This is a clear chronological structure with no random jumping between time periods.

criteria_results.title: PAA execution date correctly alleged as January 18, 2023
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 16 of the complaint explicitly states: 'On January 18, 2023, Westlake and Graydon executed the PAA...' This correctly alleges the execution date as January 18, 2023.

criteria_results.title: Demand letter and response letter referenced in factual allegations
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 47 of the complaint explicitly states that on June 3, 2024, Westlake through counsel delivered a written demand to Graydon identifying the breaches and demanding repayment, and that on June 18, 2024, Graydon through counsel rejected every demand. This satisfies the criterion requiring reference to both the demand letter and the response letter.

criteria_results.title: Issues memo identifies Graydon's anticipated defenses from response letter
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly addresses both anticipated defenses from Graydon's June 18 response letter. In Section 10 ('Anticipated Defenses and Counterclaim Exposure'), the memo discusses: (1) the 'Separate entity / § 7.4 does not reach affiliates' defense, explaining how §7.4's last sentences and §1.1's 25%-ownership prong defeat it; and (2) 'Independent investor decisions (causation)' described as 'Graydon's strongest defense on lost fees and carry,' noting the need for investor testimony. The memo also references Graydon's June 18 letter in Section 5 regarding the voluntary-payment rule argument. Both required defenses are clearly identified and analyzed.

criteria_results.title: Issues memo produced as separate deliverable
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced a detailed, standalone filing issues memo (filing-issues-memo.docx) that is clearly separate from the complaint itself (referenced as federal-complaint.docx). The memo identifies legal risks (diversity jurisdiction problems, limitations issues, economic-loss rule), strategic considerations (whether to name certain defendants, preliminary injunction timing, damages approach), and potential vulnerabilities (voluntary payment rule, reliance issues, counterclaim exposure) for the supervising partner. It is not embedded within the complaint but is a distinct deliverable addressed to the partner.

criteria_results.title: Milestone misrepresentation specifics: Actual vs. reported figures
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint provides specific actual vs. reported figures for multiple milestones. For the May 2023 ($50M) milestone: reported ~$50.5M, actual Capital Commitments $35M, and notes Graydon's own figure should have been no more than ~$42.5M. For the September 2023 ($100M) milestone: reported ~$101.5M, actual Capital Commitments still $35M. For the March 2024 ($150M) milestone: reported ~$152M, actual Capital Commitments $87.5M, and notes that without the phantom $40M in diverted prospects, Graydon's own figure falls to ~$112M. The criterion requires specific actual-vs.-reported figures for at least two milestones. The complaint provides these for all three milestones, including the ~$42.5M figure for the first milestone and the ~$112M figure for the third milestone, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Exclusivity period correctly alleged as 18 months
criteria_results.reasoning: Paragraph 16 states: 'On January 18, 2023, Westlake and Graydon executed the PAA, under which Westlake appointed Graydon as its "sole and exclusive placement agent" for Fund III (PAA §§ 2.1--2.2)... The PAA's Term ran eighteen months, through July 18, 2024 (§ 3.1).' This correctly alleges an 18-month exclusivity period from January 18, 2023 through July 18, 2024.

criteria_results.title: Complaint properly references documentary sources
criteria_results.reasoning: The complaint references: (1) the Placement Agent Agreement (PAA) extensively throughout, with specific section citations; (2) Graydon's monthly activity reports (September 9, 2023; January 9, 2024; March 8, 2024; May 8, 2023 certification); (3) the Graydon-Ridgecrest Capital Introduction Agreement (the 'Ridgecrest Agreement' described in detail in paragraphs 26-29). The fourth category, 'Millhaven investigation findings,' is not referenced anywhere in the complaint. However, three of the four document categories are clearly referenced, which meets the criterion's threshold of at least three of four.
